lead: A search radar sweeps a volume and reports whatever it finds. A tracking radar stays on one target and follows it, with a servo loop that keeps the antenna pointed at it. The loop needs an angle error signal: zero when the antenna points exactly at the target, changing sign when the target drifts to the other side. Sequential lobing, conical scan and monopulse are three ways to make it; monopulse gets it from a single pulse, which is why missile seekers and precision instrumentation radars use it.
prereq: You need antenna beams and beamwidth from Antenna fundamentals and radiation, and magic tees and hybrids from Microwave components, devices and measurements.

blocks.text: A tracking radar closes a loop: antenna, receiver, angle error detector, servo amplifier, motor and back to the antenna. The boresight (tracking axis) is the direction in which the error is zero. For a tracker this is not the peak of one beam: it is the crossover of the squinted beams, or the rotation axis of a conical scan.

blocks.where: ε is the angle error signal (a voltage, or a ratio in monopulse); θ is the angle of the target off boresight in degrees; k is the error slope, steeper for a narrower beam.

blocks.text: The servo turns the antenna until ε is zero, and keeps doing so as the target moves. Its bandwidth must be wide enough to follow a manoeuvring aircraft and narrow enough to average out receiver noise.

Sequential lobing (lobe switching) switches between two beams squinted either side of boresight. A target on boresight gives equal echoes in both; off to one side, the nearer beam gives the larger echo:

ε = (A1 − A2) / (A1 + A2)
Here A1 and A2 are the echo amplitudes in the two beams; for example 1.1 and 0.9 give ε = 0.2/2.0 = 0.1. Dividing by the sum makes ε independent of echo strength. A second pair of beams gives the other plane.

Conical scan uses one beam, squinted off axis and rotated about the boresight at a few tens of revolutions per second, so the beam traces a cone. A target on the axis gives a steady echo. Off axis, the echo rises and falls once per revolution: the depth of this modulation gives how far off the target is, and its phase against the rotation gives which way.

Both methods compare echoes taken at different times. If the target's echo fluctuates between those times, that fluctuation looks like an angle error and adds angle noise; target fluctuations often have energy at a few to tens of hertz, right where the scan rate sits. Conical scan also has a known weakness: a jammer that repeats the echo modulated at the scan rate creates a false error and pulls the antenna away. Randomising the scan rate, or scanning only the receive beam while the transmit beam stays fixed (COSRO, conical scan on receive only), hides the scan rate from the jammer.

sections.h3: Monopulse: sum and difference from one pulse

blocks.text: Monopulse (simultaneous lobing) forms all the beams at once. Four horns at the focus of a reflector give four beams squinted into the four quadrants. A comparator of magic tees or hybrid rings adds and subtracts their outputs. Number the horns, seen from behind the feed, A top-left, B bottom-left, C top-right and D bottom-right:

blocks.where: Σ is the sum channel, a normal beam on boresight, used for detection and range.
Δ<sub>az</sub> is the azimuth difference: left column minus right column; zero when the target is on boresight in azimuth.
Δ<sub>el</sub> is the elevation difference: top row minus bottom row.

blocks.text: The angle comes from the ratio θ = (Δ/Σ)/k, with k now a slope in "per degree" found by calibration. Dividing by Σ makes the reading independent of range, target size and transmitter power, and the sign of Δ/Σ gives the side. Because every channel sees the same pulse, echo fluctuation cannot create an angle error. The cost is three matched receiver channels and a more complex feed. Phase-comparison monopulse uses two side-by-side apertures with parallel beams and reads the angle from the phase difference between them; the normalisation and the servo are the same.

The range must be tracked too. A split gate puts an early gate and a late gate on either side of the echo; if the echo slides later, the late gate collects more energy, and the difference moves both gates until they balance. If the echo is lost, the tracker coasts on its last speed (memory) until the target returns. Thermal noise sets a random angle error that shrinks as S/N and the slope k grow. Glint, the wandering of the apparent centre as echoes from different parts of an aircraft add and cancel, is often larger at short range.

examples.question: A monopulse radar reads Δ<sub>az</sub> = 1.2 V and Σ = 10 V on the same pulse; its calibrated slope is k = 1.8 per degree. (a) Find Δ/Σ and the angle error. (b) Find the cross-range offset of the target at 20 km. (c) What does the servo do?
steps: The servo turns the antenna 0.0667° toward the side given by the sign of Δ/Σ, until Δ<sub>az</sub> is zero.
examples.answer: Δ/Σ = 0.12; the target is 0.0667° (23.3 m at 20 km) off boresight, and the servo turns the antenna by that amount to null the difference channel.

traps: Using Δ alone as the error. Without dividing by Σ the reading changes with echo strength, range and target size.
Reading "monopulse" as one beam. It means one pulse; it needs several squinted beams, a comparator and parallel receivers.
Swapping depth and phase in conical scan. The depth gives how far off, the phase gives which way.
Mixing degrees and radians in the slope k, an error of 57.3 times.
Defining boresight as the gain peak of the antenna. For a tracker it is the axis where the error signal is zero.

quiz.q: Define boresight for a tracking antenna and state the error signal there.
quiz.a: The tracking axis: the crossover of the squinted beams (or the rotation axis of a conical scan), where the angle error signal, and the monopulse difference channel, is zero.

quiz.q: Name the three channels a monopulse comparator forms from four squinted beams.
quiz.a: The sum Σ = A + B + C + D, the azimuth difference Δ<sub>az</sub> = (A + B) − (C + D) and the elevation difference Δ<sub>el</sub> = (A + C) − (B + D), with A, B the left column and A, C the top row.

quiz.q: Why is Δ/Σ used as the error signal rather than Δ alone?
quiz.a: Both Δ and Σ scale with echo strength, so their ratio depends only on the angle off boresight, not on range, cross section or transmitter power.

quiz.q: Why can conical scan work with one receiver while amplitude-comparison monopulse needs three?
quiz.a: Conical scan puts the angle information on one beam as a modulation in time, so one receiver sees it all. Monopulse forms Σ, Δ<sub>az</sub> and Δ<sub>el</sub> on the same pulse, so each needs its own matched channel.

quiz.q: A monopulse radar gives Σ = 8 V and Δ = 0.4 V with k = 2.0 per degree. Find Δ/Σ and the angle error.
quiz.a: Δ/Σ = 0.4/8 = 0.05; θ = 0.05/2.0 = 0.025°, and the servo moves the antenna 0.025° to null Δ.

quiz.q: A target's echo fluctuates strongly from pulse to pulse. Rank the three trackers by the angle noise this causes.
quiz.a: Sequential lobing is worst: its beams are sampled on different pulses. Conical scan also suffers, since fluctuation near the scan rate looks like an angle error. Monopulse is not affected, because all channels come from the same pulse.

quiz.q: A jammer sends a signal modulated at the conical-scan rate. Explain the effect and two counters.
quiz.a: The tracker cannot tell the false modulation from a real angle error, so the servo is pulled off target. Counters: a randomised or swept scan rate, or COSRO (only the receive beam scans), so the jammer does not know the rate; or monopulse, which has no scan to copy.

beyond: Phased-array radars form sum and difference beams digitally from many elements and track several targets at once while still searching (track-while-scan). The same sum-difference idea points satellite ground stations and guides missile seekers. Tracking filters such as the alpha-beta and Kalman filters smooth the noisy angle and range readings. Search for "monopulse comparator", "angle glint" and "Kalman tracking filter" to go further.
